claim: Visual field maps in human early extrastriate areas (V2 and V3) are traditionally thought to form mirror-image representations which surround the primary visual cortex (V1).
source: Visual field maps in human early extrastriate areas (V2 and V3) are traditionally thought to form mirror-image representations which surround the primary visual cortex (V1).
evidence: This is a statement about the traditional view in the field, representing established scientific consensus.

claim: According to the traditional scheme, V2 and V3 form nearly symmetrical halves with respect to the calcarine sulcus, with the dorsal halves representing lower contralateral quadrants, and the ventral halves representing upper contralateral quadrants.
source: According to this scheme, V2 and V3 form nearly symmetrical halves with respect to the calcarine sulcus, with the dorsal halves representing lower contralateral quadrants, and the ventral halves representing upper contralateral quadrants.
evidence: This describes the canonical model of V2 and V3 organization, representing established knowledge in the field.

claim: The traditional arrangement of V2 and V3 is considered to be consistent across individuals and predictable with reasonable accuracy using templates.
source: This arrangement is considered to be consistent across individuals, and thus predictable with reasonable accuracy using templates.
evidence: This statement describes the prevailing view in the field about inter-individual consistency.

claim: Data that deviate from the expected pattern of V2 and V3 organization have been observed but mainly treated as artifactual.
source: However, data that deviate from this expected pattern have been observed, but mainly treated as artifactual.
evidence: This is a statement about how deviations have been historically interpreted in the field.

claim: The study used the 7T Human Connectome Project (HCP) retinotopy dataset to investigate individual variability in visual field maps of human early visual cortex.
source: Here, we systematically investigate individual variability in the visual field maps of human early visual cortex using the 7T Human Connectome Project (HCP) retinotopy dataset.
evidence: This describes the dataset used in the study.

claim: Visual field representation in the dorsal portions of V2 and V3 was more variable than in their ventral counterparts.
source: Visual field representation in the dorsal portions of V2 and V3 was more variable than in their ventral counterparts, including substantial departures from the expected mirror-symmetrical patterns.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's analysis of the HCP dataset.

claim: Left hemisphere retinotopic maps were more variable than those in the right hemisphere.
source: In addition, left hemisphere retinotopic maps were more variable than those in the right hemisphere.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's analysis showing hemispheric differences.

claim: Only one-third of individuals had maps that conformed to the expected pattern in the left hemisphere.
source: Surprisingly, only one-third of individuals had maps that conformed to the expected pattern in the left hemisphere.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the study's analysis of individual variability.

claim: In many individuals, the area conventionally identified as dorsal V3 shows a discontinuity in the mirror-image representation of the retina, associated with a Y-shaped lower vertical representation.
source: Visual field sign analysis further revealed that in many individuals the area conventionally identified as dorsal V3 shows a discontinuity in the mirror-image representation of the retina, associated with a Y-shaped lower vertical representation.
evidence: This is a finding from visual field sign analysis performed in the study.

claim: The findings challenge the current view that inter-individual variability in early extrastriate cortex is negligible.
source: Our findings challenge the current view that inter-individual variability in early extrastriate cortex is negligible, and that the dorsal portions of V2 and V3 are roughly mirror images of their ventral counterparts.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the study's findings in relation to existing views.

claim: The findings challenge the view that the dorsal portions of V2 and V3 are roughly mirror images of their ventral counterparts.
source: Our findings challenge the current view that inter-individual variability in early extrastriate cortex is negligible, and that the dorsal portions of V2 and V3 are roughly mirror images of their ventral counterparts.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the study's findings in relation to the canonical model.

claim: Non-invasive imaging has been instrumental in mapping the topographic organization of human visual cortex.
source: Non-invasive imaging has been instrumental in mapping the topographic organization of human visual cortex (Wandell and Winawer, 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Visual field maps in early visual areas (V1, V2, and V3) have been reported to be remarkably consistent across people.
source: The visual field maps in early visual areas (V1, V2, and V3) have been reported to be remarkably consistent across people, and predictable with reasonable accuracy using a template (Benson et al., 2014; Benson et al., 2012; Schira et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: V1 contains a complete, first-order (continuous) representation of the contralateral visual hemifield.
source: While V1 contains a complete, first-order (continuous) representation of the contralateral visual hemifield, areas V2 and V3 form second-order (discontinuous) representations (Rosa, 2002).
evidence: This is a statement about the organization of V1, supported by a citation.

claim: Areas V2 and V3 form second-order (discontinuous) representations.
source: While V1 contains a complete, first-order (continuous) representation of the contralateral visual hemifield, areas V2 and V3 form second-order (discontinuous) representations (Rosa, 2002).
evidence: This is a statement about the organization of V2 and V3, supported by a citation.

claim: In V2 and V3, a field discontinuity near the horizontal meridian splits the maps into upper and lower field representations that are only connected at the foveal confluence.
source: In these areas, a field discontinuity near the horizontal meridian splits the maps into upper and lower field representations that are only connected at the foveal confluence (Figure 1a, b).
evidence: This describes the organization of V2 and V3, with reference to Figure 1.

claim: In parcellation schemes, early visual areas form concentric bands, arranged in nearly symmetrical halves with respect to the calcarine sulcus.
source: Accordingly, in parcellation schemes (Glasser et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2015), early visual areas form concentric bands, arranged in nearly symmetrical halves with respect to the calcarine sulcus.
evidence: This describes the organization in existing parcellation schemes, supported by citations.

claim: Observations from several laboratories have indicated departures from the canonical pattern, particularly in the dorsal region.
source: However, observations originating in several laboratories have indicated departures from this pattern, particularly in the dorsal region (Allen et al., 2022; Arcaro and Kastner, 2015; Benson and Winawer, 2018; Van Essen and Glasser, 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to multiple previous studies.

claim: Small-sized datasets, variability in acquisition sites and protocols, and methodological constraints have limited the investigation of variability in V2 and V3 organization.
source: Even so, small-sized datasets, variability in acquisition sites and protocols, and methodological constraints have limited the investigation of this variability.
evidence: This is an inference about why variability has not been systematically studied.

claim: No consensus exists about deviations from the canonical mirror-symmetrical organization of V2 and V3.
source: As a result, no consensus exists about deviations from the canonical mirror-symmetrical organization of V2 and V3.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of the field.

claim: In primates, isoangle bands representing the vertical and the horizontal meridians are thought to delineate boundaries between V1 and V2, V2 and V3, and V3 and higher-order visual areas.
source: In primates, isoangle bands representing the vertical and the horizontal meridians are thought to delineate boundaries between V1 and V2, V2 and V3, and V3 and higher-order visual areas (Figure 1b).
evidence: This describes the conventional understanding of visual area boundaries in primates.

claim: In human probabilistic maps, boundaries between the dorsal portions of early visual areas are roughly mirror images of their ventral counterparts.
source: Particularly, in human probabilistic maps, boundaries between the dorsal portions of early visual areas are roughly mirror images of their ventral counterparts (Figure 1c).
evidence: This describes the organization in probabilistic maps, with reference to Figure 1c.

claim: Boundaries that deviate from the expected ones exist, but these have been mainly treated as artifactual, with researchers often overlooking the irregularities by drawing boundaries to resemble a canonical map.
source: Nevertheless, boundaries that deviate from the expected ones exist, but these have been mainly treated as artifactual, with researchers often overlooking the irregularities by simply drawing the boundaries to resemble that of a canonical map as best as possible (e.g., Figure 1d).
evidence: This describes how deviations have been historically handled, with reference to Figure 1d.

claim: The border between the dorsal parts of V2 and V3 is well known to be variable in other mammals and typically does not coincide with the representation of the horizontal meridian.
source: Here, it may be important to remark that the border between the dorsal parts of V2 and V3 is well known to be variable in other mammals, and that it typically does not coincide with the representation of the horizontal meridian (see Rosa and Manger, 2005 for review).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a review article.

claim: A recently developed deep learning model predicts that individual variability in retinotopy exists and is correlated with variations in gross anatomy.
source: Although previous reports of individual variability in the dorsal portion of human early visual cortex were primarily anecdotal (Allen et al., 2022; Arcaro and Kastner, 2015; Benson and Winawer, 2018; Van Essen and Glasser, 2018), a recently developed deep learning model predicts that individual variability in retinotopy exists, and that this is correlated with variations in gross anatomy (e.g., the pattern of sulci and gyri) (Ribeiro et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Studies modeling the formation of retinotopic maps in non-human primates indicate that different variants could develop based on the application of similar developmental rules.
source: Moreover, studies modeling the formation of retinotopic maps in non-human primates also indicate that different variants could develop based on the application of similar developmental rules (Yu et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The study used data from 181 participants in the 7T Human Connectome Project retinotopy dataset.
source: Motivated by these findings, here we systematically investigate individual variability in visual field maps of human early visual cortex using a recently released, large-scale dataset: the 181 participants, 7T Human Connectome Project (HCP) retinotopy dataset (Benson et al., 2018).
evidence: This describes the dataset used in the study.

claim: The study aimed to quantify the level of individual variability throughout early visual cortex (V1–V3).
source: Our aims were to quantify the level of individual variability throughout early visual cortex (V1–V3) and to determine whether there are common modes of retinotopic organization that differ from the established view (i.e., whether individual retinotopic maps differ from a template in similar ways).
evidence: This describes one of the study's aims.

claim: The study aimed to determine whether there are common modes of retinotopic organization that differ from the established view.
source: Our aims were to quantify the level of individual variability throughout early visual cortex (V1–V3) and to determine whether there are common modes of retinotopic organization that differ from the established view (i.e., whether individual retinotopic maps differ from a template in similar ways).
evidence: This describes one of the study's aims.

claim: The results demonstrate that the dorsal portions of human early visual areas are more heterogeneous than previously acknowledged.
source: Our results demonstrate that the dorsal portions of human early visual areas are more heterogeneous than previously acknowledged and challenge the current view that individual differences in retinotopic organization reflect experimental artifacts that may be dismissed for practical purposes.
evidence: This is a summary of the study's findings.

claim: The findings challenge the view that individual differences in retinotopic organization reflect experimental artifacts that may be dismissed for practical purposes.
source: Our results demonstrate that the dorsal portions of human early visual areas are more heterogeneous than previously acknowledged and challenge the current view that individual differences in retinotopic organization reflect experimental artifacts that may be dismissed for practical purposes.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the study's findings.

claim: The study computed average visual field maps across all 181 individuals from the HCP retinotopy dataset for both left and right hemispheres.
source: First, we computed the average visual field maps across all 181 individuals from the HCP retinotopy dataset for both left and right hemispheres.
evidence: This describes a methodological step in the analysis.

claim: Individual variability was calculated as the difference between an individual's visual field map and the average map, averaged over all vertices within the dorsal and ventral portions of early visual areas.
source: Then, we iteratively calculated the difference between an individual's visual field map and the average map. Finally, these differences were averaged over all vertices within the dorsal and ventral portions of early visual areas, resulting in one scalar value per individual per visual area, which is our individual variability metric.
evidence: This describes how the individual variability metric was calculated.

claim: A linear mixed-effect (LME) model was built to test the fixed effects of hemispheres, visual areas, and portions on large-scale individual variability of polar angle maps.
source: We built a linear mixed-effect (LME) model (Yu et al., 2022) to test the fixed effects of hemispheres, visual areas, and portions on large-scale individual variability of polar angle (Table 1) and eccentricity (Table 2) maps.
evidence: This describes the statistical analysis method used.

claim: There were statistically significant main effects of all factors (hemisphere, visual area, and portion) on individual variability of polar angle maps.
source: Table 1 shows statistically significant main effects of all factors on individual variability of polar angle maps.
evidence: This is a finding from the statistical analysis, as shown in Table 1.

claim: Polar angle maps of the left hemisphere show higher individual variability than those found in the right hemisphere (mean difference = 3.35, p < 0.001).
source: Specifically, polar angle maps of the left hemisphere show higher individual variability than those found in the right hemisphere (mean difference = 3.35, p < 0.001).
evidence: This is a specific finding from the statistical analysis.

claim: The dorsal portions of early visual areas are more variable than the ventral portions (mean difference = 3.30, p < 0.001).
source: The dorsal portions of early visual areas are also more variable than the ventral portions (mean difference = 3.30, p < 0.001).
evidence: This is a specific finding from the statistical analysis.

claim: V3 has higher individual variability than V2 (mean difference = 1.60, p < 0.001).
source: Finally, post hoc comparisons of visual areas indicated that V3 has higher individual variability than V2 (mean difference = 1.60, p < 0.001) and V1 (mean difference = 3.99, p < 0.001); V2 also has higher individual variability than V1 (mean difference = 2.38, p < 0.001).
evidence: This is a specific finding from post hoc comparisons.

claim: V3 has higher individual variability than V1 (mean difference = 3.99, p < 0.001).
source: Finally, post hoc comparisons of visual areas indicated that V3 has higher individual variability than V2 (mean difference = 1.60, p < 0.001) and V1 (mean difference = 3.99, p < 0.001); V2 also has higher individual variability than V1 (mean difference = 2.38, p < 0.001).
evidence: This is a specific finding from post hoc comparisons.

claim: V2 has higher individual variability than V1 (mean difference = 2.38, p < 0.001).
source: Finally, post hoc comparisons of visual areas indicated that V3 has higher individual variability than V2 (mean difference = 1.60, p < 0.001) and V1 (mean difference = 3.99, p < 0.001); V2 also has higher individual variability than V1 (mean difference = 2.38, p < 0.001).
evidence: This is a specific finding from post hoc comparisons.

claim: Each visual area in the left hemisphere has significantly higher individual variability than its analogous area in the right hemisphere.
source: Briefly, each visual area in the left hemisphere has significantly higher individual variability than its analogous area in the right hemisphere.
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis of interactions.

claim: The dorsal portion of each visual area of the left hemisphere is significantly more variable than its dorsal analog in the right hemisphere and the ventral analog of both the left and right hemispheres.
source: In addition, the dorsal portion of each visual area of the left hemisphere is significantly more variable than its dorsal analog in the right hemisphere and the ventral analog of both the left and right hemispheres (for more, see Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis of interactions.

claim: Individual variability in polar angle representations varies across hemispheres, visual areas, and according to dorsal/ventral locations.
source: These findings suggest that individual variability in polar angle representations varies across hemispheres, visual areas, and according to dorsal/ventral locations.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the statistical findings.

claim: There were statistically significant main effects of the hemisphere, visual area, and the visual area portion on individual variability of eccentricity maps.
source: Moreover, Table 2 shows statistically significant main effects of the hemisphere, visual area, and the visual area portion on individual variability of eccentricity maps.
evidence: This is a finding from the statistical analysis, as shown in Table 2.

claim: Eccentricity maps of the left hemisphere show higher individual variability than those in the right hemisphere (mean difference = 0.14, p < 0.001).
source: Like polar angle maps, eccentricity maps of the left hemisphere show higher individual variability than those in the right hemisphere (mean difference = 0.14, p < 0.001).
evidence: This is a specific finding from the statistical analysis.

claim: The dorsal portion of early visual areas is more variable than the ventral portion for eccentricity maps (mean difference = 0.13, p < 0.001).
source: The dorsal portion of early visual areas is also more variable than the ventral portion (mean difference = 0.13, p < 0.001).
evidence: This is a specific finding from the statistical analysis.

claim: For eccentricity maps, the only statistically significant difference among visual areas was that V3 has higher individual variability than V1 (mean difference = 0.05, p < 0.004).
source: For visual areas, post hoc comparisons indicated that the only statistically significant difference was that of V3 versus V1, with V3 having higher individual variability than V1 (mean difference = 0.05, p < 0.004).
evidence: This is a specific finding from post hoc comparisons.

claim: Each visual area in the left hemisphere has significantly higher individual variability in eccentricity maps than analogous areas in the right hemisphere, except for V3.
source: Each visual area in the left hemisphere has significantly higher individual variability than analogous areas in the right hemisphere, except for V3.
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis of interactions for eccentricity maps.

claim: Eccentricity maps of each visual area's dorsal portion in the left hemisphere are significantly more variable than the dorsal counterpart in the right hemisphere, and the ventral analogs in both the left and the right hemispheres.
source: Eccentricity maps of each visual area's dorsal portion in the left hemisphere are significantly more variable than the dorsal counterpart in the right hemisphere, and the ventral analogs in both the left and the right hemispheres.
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis of interactions for eccentricity maps.

claim: Cortical curvature and mean blood oxygenation level dependent (BOLD) signal are known to be correlated with retinotopy.
source: As mentioned in the Materials and methods, these factors are known to be correlated with retinotopy and could explain part of the variability found across visual areas.
evidence: This is a statement about known relationships in the field.

claim: Across V1–3, polar angle was significantly correlated with curvature and the mean BOLD signal in both the right and left hemispheres.
source: Across V1–3 (Figure 3, main plots), polar angle was significantly correlated with curvature and the mean BOLD signal in both the right and left hemispheres; eccentricity was correlated with the mean BOLD signal in both hemispheres and curvature in the right hemisphere.
evidence: This is a finding from the correlation analysis, as shown in Figure 3.

claim: Eccentricity was correlated with the mean BOLD signal in both hemispheres and curvature in the right hemisphere.
source: Across V1–3 (Figure 3, main plots), polar angle was significantly correlated with curvature and the mean BOLD signal in both the right and left hemispheres; eccentricity was correlated with the mean BOLD signal in both hemispheres and curvature in the right hemisphere.
evidence: This is a finding from the correlation analysis, as shown in Figure 3.

claim: The correlation between polar angle, eccentricity, curvature, and mean BOLD signal varied across visual areas.
source: Moreover, the correlation between these maps varied across visual areas. Specifically, correlations between polar angle and curvature, polar angle and mean BOLD signal, and curvature and mean BOLD signal decreased from V1 to V2 to V3.
evidence: This is a finding from the correlation analysis.

claim: Correlations between polar angle and curvature, polar angle and mean BOLD signal, and curvature and mean BOLD signal decreased from V1 to V2 to V3.
source: Specifically, correlations between polar angle and curvature, polar angle and mean BOLD signal, and curvature and mean BOLD signal decreased from V1 to V2 to V3.
evidence: This is a specific finding from the correlation analysis.

claim: The main effects of all factors (hemispheres, visual areas, and portions) on individual variability of polar angle maps persisted after accounting for covariates, but the estimated effects were slightly reduced.
source: Our findings indicate that the main effects found here were not a mere reflection of variation in the reliability of the individual maps and other covariates, at least at large scale. For example, we found that the main effects of all factors (hemispheres, visual areas, and portions) on individual variability of polar angle maps persisted, but the estimated effects were slightly reduced (Table 3).
evidence: This is a finding from the LME model with covariates.

claim: For eccentricity, the main effects of hemisphere and portion but not visual area were found after accounting for covariates.
source: For eccentricity, we found the main effects of hemisphere and portion but not visual area after accounting for these covariates (Table 4).
evidence: This is a finding from the LME model with covariates.

claim: Individual variability in polar angle representations varies as a function of hemispheres, visual areas, and dorsal/ventral locations, and these effects are not only due to trivial intra-individual variability in pRF estimates or individual variability in curvature and the mean BOLD signal.
source: Crucially, these findings suggest that individual variability in polar angle representations varies as a function of hemispheres, visual areas, and dorsal/ventral locations. These effects are not only due to trivial intra-individual variability in pRF estimates or individual variability in curvature and the mean BOLD signal.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings from the LME model with covariates.

claim: Average maps from clusters 1 and 5 capture nearly a third of individuals and show canonical polar angle representations.
source: Specifically, average maps from clusters 1 and 5 capture nearly a third of individuals and show canonical polar angle representations, with clear boundaries between V1/V2 and V2/V3 (Figure 1c and Figure 4c).
evidence: This is a finding from the clustering analysis, as shown in Figure 4c.

claim: Clusters 2, 3, and 4 capture nearly two-thirds of individuals and deviate from the canonical polar angle representation.
source: However, clusters 2, 3, and 4 capture nearly two-thirds of individuals and deviate from this canonical polar angle representation (Figure 4c).
evidence: This is a finding from the clustering analysis, as shown in Figure 4c.

claim: The average map from cluster 2 shows that the boundaries between V1 and V2, and the most anterior portion of V3 and higher-order visual areas, merge to form a Y-shaped (or forked) lower vertical representation.
source: The average map from cluster 2 shows that the boundaries between V1 and V2, and the most anterior portion of V3 and higher-order visual areas, merge to form a Y-shaped (or forked) lower vertical representation.
evidence: This is a description of the average map from cluster 2.

claim: Clusters 3 and 4 show a truncated V3 boundary, indicating that dorsal V3 does not cover the entire quarter visual field.
source: Clusters 3 and 4 show a truncated V3 boundary, indicating that dorsal V3 does not cover the entire quarter visual field (i.e., from 360° to 270°) either throughout its length or only in its most anterior portion.
evidence: This is a description of the average maps from clusters 3 and 4.

claim: Cluster 6 reflects unclear retinotopic organization, with a handful of individuals' retinotopic maps showing overall low correspondence with the canonical retinotopic organization.
source: Finally, cluster 6 reflects unclear retinotopic organization, with a handful of individuals' retinotopic maps showing overall low correspondence with the canonical retinotopic organization.
evidence: This is a description of cluster 6.

claim: The average within-cluster Jaccard score is 0.54 (standard deviation = 0.07), while the average between-cluster score is 0.46 (standard deviation = 0.08).
source: Despite this, we found that the average within-cluster Jaccard score is 0.54 (standard deviation (SD) = 0.07), while the average between-cluster score is 0.46 (SD = 0.08), showing that pairs of maps within a cluster are, on average, more similar than between clusters.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the clustering analysis.

claim: Pairs of maps within a cluster are, on average, more similar than between clusters.
source: Despite this, we found that the average within-cluster Jaccard score is 0.54 (standard deviation (SD) = 0.07), while the average between-cluster score is 0.46 (SD = 0.08), showing that pairs of maps within a cluster are, on average, more similar than between clusters.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the Jaccard scores.

claim: Visual field sign analysis combines both polar angle and eccentricity maps into a unique representation of the visual field as either a non-mirror-image or a mirror-image representation of the retina.
source: To do so, we performed a visual field sign analysis (Sereno et al., 1995; Sereno et al., 1994), which combines both polar angle and eccentricity maps into a unique representation of the visual field as either a non-mirror-image or a mirror-image representation of the retina (Figure 7a; see Materials and methods).
evidence: This describes the visual field sign analysis method, supported by citations.

claim: The visual field sign representation reveals that the area identified as dorsal V3 shows a discontinuity in the canonical mirror-image representation in individuals with non-canonical maps.
source: However, with the visual field sign representation, the boundaries delineating dorsal V2 in those participants with non-canonical maps are more explicit, and it reveals that the area identified as dorsal V3 shows a discontinuity in the expected mirror-image representation.
evidence: This is a finding from the visual field sign analysis.

claim: The discontinuous representation in dorsal V3 has been proposed as the 'incomplete-V3' model of the third-tier cortex for the macaque.
source: Such representation has been proposed as the 'incomplete-V3' model of the third-tier cortex for the macaque (Angelucci and Rosa, 2015) and other similar models for the owl monkey (Sereno et al., 2015) and the marmoset monkey (Rosa and Tweedale, 2000).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Individuals with unusual Y-shaped lower vertical representations have a discontinuity in the canonical mirror-image representation of the retina in dorsal V3.
source: While individuals with unusual Y-shaped lower vertical representations have a discontinuity in the canonical mirror-image representation of the retina in dorsal V3, individuals with a truncated V3 do not show such a discontinuity.
evidence: This is a finding from the visual field sign analysis.

claim: Individuals with a truncated V3 do not show a discontinuity in the canonical mirror-image representation.
source: While individuals with unusual Y-shaped lower vertical representations have a discontinuity in the canonical mirror-image representation of the retina in dorsal V3, individuals with a truncated V3 do not show such a discontinuity.
evidence: This is a finding from the visual field sign analysis.

claim: In humans, the canonical model does not oppose other models established for non-human primates; these models coexist and reflect common modes of variability in the retinotopic mapping of early visual areas.
source: Altogether, our findings may suggest that, at least in humans, the canonical model does not oppose other models established for non-human primates; these models coexist and reflect common modes of variability in the retinotopic mapping of early visual areas.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings in relation to models from non-human primates.

claim: Retinotopic maps in the left hemisphere were more variable than those in the right hemisphere.
source: We found that retinotopic maps in the left hemisphere were more variable than those in the right hemisphere.
evidence: This is a summary of a primary finding from the study.

claim: In the left hemisphere, the dorsal portions of early visual areas were more variable than their ventral counterparts.
source: Moreover, in the left hemisphere the dorsal portions of early visual areas were more variable than their ventral counterparts, and these effects were not merely due to trivial large-scale intra-individual variability in pRF estimates or individual variability in curvature and the mean BOLD signal.
evidence: This is a summary of a primary finding from the study.

claim: The effects of greater variability in the left hemisphere and dorsal portions were not merely due to trivial large-scale intra-individual variability in pRF estimates or individual variability in curvature and the mean BOLD signal.
source: Moreover, in the left hemisphere the dorsal portions of early visual areas were more variable than their ventral counterparts, and these effects were not merely due to trivial large-scale intra-individual variability in pRF estimates or individual variability in curvature and the mean BOLD signal.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings after controlling for covariates.

claim: Deviations from the canonical model of continuous, alternating bands of vertical and horizontal meridian representation in V2 and V3 exist in the majority of individuals.
source: This analysis showed that deviations from the canonical model of continuous, alternating bands of vertical and horizontal meridian representation in V2 and V3 exist in the majority of individuals.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from the clustering analysis.

claim: The visual field sign analysis revealed that the area identified as dorsal V3 shows a discontinuity in the expected mirror-image representation of the retina in individuals with a Y-shaped lower vertical representation in the dorsal portion of early visual cortex.
source: Specifically, the visual field sign analysis revealed that the area identified as dorsal V3 shows a discontinuity in the expected mirror-image representation of the retina in individuals with a Y-shaped lower vertical representation in the dorsal portion of early visual cortex.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from the visual field sign analysis.

claim: The findings challenge the current view that the dorsal portions of early visual areas form retinotopic maps which are consistent between individuals and are roughly mirror images of their ventral counterparts.
source: Overall, our findings challenge the current view that the dorsal portions of early visual areas form retinotopic maps which are consistent between individuals and are roughly mirror images of their ventral counterparts.
evidence: This is a summary interpretation of the study's findings.

claim: A number of studies have indicated a complex, retinotopic organization of dorsal early visual areas in non-human primates, using both electrophysiological recordings and high-resolution fMRI.
source: Although previous evidence for the variability seen across dorsal early visual cortex in humans has been mostly anecdotal, a number of studies have indicated a complex, retinotopic organization of dorsal early visual areas in non-human primates, using both electrophysiological recordings and high-resolution fMRI (Angelucci and Rosa, 2015; Gattass et al., 1988; Sereno et al., 2015; Zhu and Vanduffel, 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: There is a long-standing debate about the number of visual areas and their boundaries in the third-tier visual cortex of New and Old-World monkeys.
source: Accordingly, there is a long-standing debate about the number of visual areas – and their boundaries – in the third-tier visual cortex of New and Old-World monkeys (Angelucci and Rosa, 2015; Hadjidimitrakis et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The question of whether the areal boundaries in the third-tier visual cortex show significant individual variability has not been studied systematically in non-human primates.
source: However, the question of whether the areal boundaries in this region show significant individual variability has not been studied systematically in non-human primates.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of research in non-human primates.

claim: Gattass et al. (1988) reported in the macaque monkey that the representation of the lower vertical meridian in dorsal V3 varied across individuals.
source: Only (Gattass et al., 1988) reported, in the macaque monkey, that the representation of the lower vertical meridian in dorsal V3 varied across individuals, but firm conclusions could not be drawn due to the small sample.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Gattass et al. indicated that some animals showed a continuous representation of the lower vertical meridian along the rostral border of dorsal V3, whereas in others additional field discontinuities created a discontinuous representation.
source: These authors indicated that some animals showed a continuous representation of this meridian along the rostral border of this area, whereas in others additional field discontinuities created a discontinuous representation.
evidence: This describes findings from Gattass et al. (1988).

claim: The same discontinuities in the anterior border of dorsal V3 found by Gattass et al. were also found in the systematic investigation of individual variability in human polar angle maps.
source: Notably, the same discontinuities in the anterior border of dorsal V3 were also found in our systematic investigation of individual variability in human polar angle maps.
evidence: This connects the current findings to previous work in non-human primates.

claim: The same pattern of variation (relatively simple and reproducible representations of the upper contralateral quadrant, and complex and variable representations of the lower quadrant) characterize V2 and V3 in at least one non-primate, the cat.
source: It is also significant that the same pattern of variation (relatively simple and reproducible representations of the upper contralateral quadrant, and complex and variable representations of the lower quadrant) characterize V2 and V3 in at least one non-primate, the cat (Rosa and Manger, 2005; Tusa et al., 1979).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: A spectral clustering algorithm was applied with a fixed number of clusters equal to 6.
source: To assess whether inter-individual differences fell into stereotyped patterns, we applied a spectral clustering algorithm from Scikit-learn (Abraham et al., 2014; Pedregosa et al., 2011). This algorithm operates on the low-dimensional embedding of the affinity matrix (our Jaccard index-based similarity matrix), followed by K-means clustering of the components of the eigenvectors in the low-dimensional space. This low-dimensional space is determined by selecting the most relevant eigenvectors of the graph Laplacian of the affinity matrix, of which corresponding eigenvalues reflect important properties of the affinity matrix that can be used to partition it (von Luxburg, 2007). In implementing the spectral clustering algorithm, we set the number of clusters to 6 and fixed the random state for replication purposes.
evidence: This describes the clustering method used, supported by citations.
